subject: Science
learning_objectives: Identify the major nutrients present in food: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals
Describe the function of each nutrient in the human body
Explain the role of water and roughage (dietary fibre) in maintaining health
Perform and interpret simple tests to detect starch, protein, and fat in food samples
Identify deficiency diseases caused by lack of specific nutrients
Understand what a balanced diet is and why it is important
Connect nutrition knowledge to Karnataka's local foods and dietary practices
Answer questions using correct scientific vocabulary from the chapter
prerequisite_knowledge: Knowledge that food comes from plants and animals (Chapter 1)
Basic awareness that eating different foods keeps us healthy
Familiarity with common foods like rice, dal, milk, vegetables, and fruits
Understanding that our body needs energy to work, grow, and stay healthy

introduction.why_important: Knowing what nutrients are in our food helps us understand why we need to eat a variety of foods. A diet lacking any one nutrient can cause specific diseases. This chapter gives students the scientific foundation to make healthy food choices for life.
introduction.real_life_relevance: Every time you eat rice, dal, a banana, or drink milk, your body is receiving different chemicals — carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins — that it uses for energy, growth, and protection from disease. Understanding these nutrients explains why eating only one type of food (like only rice) makes a person unhealthy, while a varied diet keeps them well.
introduction.karnataka_context: Karnataka's traditional diet is naturally well-balanced. Ragi mudde provides carbohydrates and calcium; sambar with dal provides protein; coconut-based chutneys provide healthy fats; drumstick and leafy vegetables provide vitamins and minerals. However, vitamin A deficiency (causing night blindness) remains a health concern in rural Karnataka, and the state government runs the Vitamin A supplementation programme for children under the National Health Mission. Anaemia (iron deficiency) is also addressed through mid-day meal fortification in Karnataka's government schools.
introduction.connection_to_previous_learning: In Chapter 1, we learnt that food comes from plants and animals. Chapter 2 goes deeper — explaining what is inside that food (nutrients) and what each nutrient does for our body.

characters.name: Carbohydrates
characters.role: The primary energy-providing nutrient found in starchy and sweet foods like rice, wheat, potato, and sugar

characters.name: Proteins
characters.role: The body-building nutrient found in dal, eggs, milk, meat, and nuts — essential for growth and repair

characters.name: Fats
characters.role: The energy-storing nutrient found in oil, butter, ghee, and nuts — provides twice the energy of carbohydrates per gram

characters.name: Vitamins and Minerals
characters.role: The protective nutrients found in fruits, vegetables, and dairy — needed in small amounts but essential for preventing deficiency diseases

characters.name: Water and Roughage
characters.role: Essential non-nutrient components — water transports nutrients and regulates body temperature; roughage aids digestion and prevents constipation

plot: The chapter opens by asking why we need to eat a variety of foods rather than just one type.
It introduces the concept of nutrients — the chemical substances in food that the body needs for energy, growth, and protection.
Carbohydrates are introduced as the main energy source — found in rice, wheat, potato, sugar, and maize.
Proteins are explained as the building blocks of the body — found in dal, milk, eggs, meat, soya, and nuts.
Fats are introduced as concentrated energy stores — found in oil, butter, ghee, nuts, and some meats.
Vitamins are explained as protective nutrients needed in tiny amounts — different vitamins prevent different deficiency diseases.
Minerals like calcium (for bones) and iron (for blood) are introduced with their food sources and deficiency effects.
Water is explained as essential for all body functions — transporting nutrients, regulating temperature, and removing waste.
Roughage (dietary fibre) is explained as the indigestible plant material that helps move food through the digestive system.
Simple tests to detect starch (iodine test), protein (biuret test with copper sulphate and caustic soda), and fat (paper test) are described.
The concept of a balanced diet is introduced — a diet that includes all nutrients in the right proportions.
Deficiency diseases are listed: kwashiorkor and marasmus (protein), night blindness (Vitamin A), scurvy (Vitamin C), rickets (Vitamin D), anaemia (iron), goitre (iodine).
The chapter ends by encouraging students to evaluate their own diets for balance.
story_summary.moral: Health is not just about eating enough food — it is about eating the right variety of foods with all essential nutrients in the correct proportions. A balanced diet is the foundation of a healthy life.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: Food contains special chemicals called nutrients. Each nutrient has a specific job in our body — some give energy, some help us grow, and some protect us from disease.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: There are five major nutrients: (1) Carbohydrates — the body's primary and quickest source of energy. Found in rice, wheat, maize, potato, sugar, and bread. The body breaks carbohydrates into glucose, which powers all cells. (2) Proteins — the building blocks for growth and repair of the body. Found in dal, milk, eggs, meat, soya bean, cheese, and nuts. Essential for making new cells, muscles, and enzymes. (3) Fats — a concentrated energy store; provide more than twice the energy of carbohydrates per gram. Found in oil, butter, ghee, nuts, avocado, and fatty meats. Also help absorb fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). (4) Vitamins — needed in very small amounts but essential for specific body functions. Vitamin A (eyes/skin), Vitamin B (energy metabolism), Vitamin C (immunity, wound healing), Vitamin D (bones), Vitamin K (blood clotting). (5) Minerals — inorganic elements needed for specific functions. Calcium (strong bones and teeth), Iron (makes haemoglobin for blood), Iodine (thyroid hormone production).
core_concepts.real_life_example: Think of your body as a car: carbohydrates are the petrol (fuel for energy), proteins are the steel and rubber (for building and repairing parts), fats are the reserve fuel tank, vitamins and minerals are the engine oil and coolant (small amounts but essential for everything to work), and water is the radiator fluid that keeps everything running smoothly.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Karnataka's traditional ragi mudde with sambar is a near-perfect nutrient combination: ragi provides carbohydrates and calcium (mineral), sambar's toor dal provides protein, the coconut used in many Karnataka dishes provides healthy fats, and the drumstick and tomatoes in sambar provide vitamins C and A. The Karnataka government's mid-day meal programme in government schools provides iron-fortified rice to address anaemia (iron deficiency) — a nutrition intervention directly linked to this chapter's content.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students often think fats are always bad and should be avoided. In fact, fats are an essential nutrient — they provide energy, insulate the body, protect organs, and help absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K. The problem is excess fat consumption, not fat itself. Similarly, students sometimes confuse carbohydrates with only sweet foods — starchy foods like rice, bread, and potato are also carbohydrates.
core_concepts.memory_tip: Remember 'CPF-VM-WR': Carbohydrates (energy), Proteins (building), Fats (reserve energy), Vitamins (protection), Minerals (structure), Water (transport), Roughage (digestion). Or use the sentence: 'Can People Find Very Many Wild Rabbits?' = C-P-F-V-M-W-R.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: We can test food to find out which nutrients are present using simple chemical tests — iodine for starch, a paper test for fats, and copper sulphate solution for proteins.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Three important nutrient tests are taught in this chapter: (1) Iodine test for starch — when iodine solution (iodine dissolved in potassium iodide) is added to a food sample containing starch, it turns blue-black. If there is no starch, iodine remains its original orange-brown colour. Rice, potato, and bread test positive. (2) Paper test for fat — when a food sample is rubbed on plain white paper and held against the light, a greasy, translucent (see-through) patch indicates the presence of fat. Oil, butter, groundnut, and ghee test positive. (3) Biuret test for protein — when copper sulphate solution and caustic soda (sodium hydroxide) solution are added to a food sample, a violet/purple colour indicates the presence of protein. Egg white, milk, and dal test positive.
core_concepts.real_life_example: You can try a simple version of the fat test at home: rub a small piece of groundnut or a drop of oil on a piece of plain paper. Hold the paper against a window. You will see a translucent (oily, see-through) patch — this confirms fat is present. Try the same with a piece of apple — no translucent patch, so apple has little or no fat.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Groundnut (shengdana) is widely grown and consumed in northern Karnataka districts like Kalaburagi and Bidar. When you test groundnut using the paper test, it shows a strong positive result for fat — confirming that groundnuts are a rich source of fat and protein. This test can be performed with locally available Karnataka foods in a school science lab, making it directly relevant and culturally meaningful for students.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students often confuse the iodine test result: iodine turns BLUE-BLACK in the presence of starch (not red or green). The original colour of iodine solution is orange-brown, and this is the negative result. Also, the fat test result is a translucent (oily, see-through) patch — not a wet patch. Water also creates a wet patch but it dries up; a fat patch remains permanently.
core_concepts.memory_tip: Tests in three colours: Iodine test = Blue-Black (starch present). Biuret test = Violet/Purple (protein present). Fat test = Translucent patch (fat present). 'Blue for starch, Purple for protein, Transparent for fat' — BPT.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: When the body does not get enough of a specific nutrient for a long time, it causes a deficiency disease. Eating a balanced diet — with all nutrients in the right amounts — prevents these diseases.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Each nutrient deficiency causes a distinct disease: (1) Protein deficiency — Kwashiorkor (swollen belly, thin limbs in children) and Marasmus (severe wasting of muscles, extremely thin body). (2) Vitamin A deficiency — Night blindness (inability to see in dim light) and dry, rough skin. (3) Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency — Beriberi (weakness, nerve damage). (4) Vitamin C deficiency — Scurvy (bleeding gums, slow wound healing). (5) Vitamin D deficiency — Rickets in children (soft, bent bones) and Osteomalacia in adults. (6) Iron deficiency — Anaemia (low haemoglobin, fatigue, pale skin). (7) Iodine deficiency — Goitre (swelling of thyroid gland in the neck). A balanced diet contains all five nutrients plus water and roughage in proportions appropriate for the person's age, sex, and activity level. No single food provides all nutrients — variety is essential.
core_concepts.real_life_example: If a child eats only rice every day without any dal, vegetables, or milk, they may develop kwashiorkor (protein deficiency) — their belly swells while their limbs become thin. If someone avoids all fruits and vegetables for months, they may develop scurvy — their gums bleed and wounds heal slowly. These are not historical diseases — they still occur in India among children with very limited diets.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Night blindness (Vitamin A deficiency) is a documented public health concern in rural Karnataka. The Karnataka government runs a Vitamin A supplementation programme under the National Health Mission for children between 9 months and 5 years. Anaemia (iron deficiency) is addressed through the distribution of iron and folic acid tablets in Karnataka's schools and the fortification of rice distributed through mid-day meal programmes. Iodine deficiency was common in Karnataka's inland districts before iodised salt became mandatory — a direct real-world connection to goitre prevention.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students often mix up the deficiency disease with the wrong nutrient. The most common errors are: confusing night blindness (Vitamin A deficiency) with Vitamin C or D; confusing rickets (Vitamin D) with scurvy (Vitamin C); and confusing anaemia (iron deficiency) with goitre (iodine deficiency). Make a table to keep these straight. Also, 'balanced diet' does not mean eating equal amounts of everything — it means eating the right proportions of each nutrient type.
core_concepts.memory_tip: Use this table mnemonic — 'Proteins KM, A-Night, C-Scurvy, D-Rickets, Iron-Anaemia, Iodine-Goitre': Proteins → KM (Kwashiorkor, Marasmus), Vitamin A → Night blindness, Vitamin C → Scurvy, Vitamin D → Rickets, Iron → Anaemia, Iodine → Goitre. PANCI-IG.

key_terms_glossary.meaning: A chemical substance present in food that the body needs for energy, growth, repair, and protection from disease. The five major nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals.
The primary energy-providing nutrient found in starchy and sweet foods like rice, wheat, potato, and sugar. The body breaks carbohydrates into glucose for immediate energy.
The body-building nutrient essential for growth, repair, and making enzymes and antibodies. Found in dal, eggs, milk, meat, soya bean, and nuts. Deficiency causes kwashiorkor and marasmus.
A concentrated energy-storing nutrient that also helps absorb vitamins and insulates the body. Found in oils, butter, ghee, and nuts. Provides more than twice the energy of carbohydrates per gram.

An organic nutrient needed in very small amounts for specific body functions. Examples: Vitamin A (vision), Vitamin C (immunity), Vitamin D (bone strength). Deficiency of each vitamin causes a specific disease.

An inorganic nutrient needed for specific body functions. Calcium builds bones and teeth; iron makes haemoglobin in blood; iodine is needed for thyroid hormone. Deficiency causes anaemia (iron) and goitre (iodine).

The indigestible portion of plant food (mostly cellulose) that aids movement of food through the digestive system, prevents constipation, and supports gut health. Found in whole grains, vegetables, and fruits.
A diet that contains all essential nutrients — carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water, and roughage — in the correct proportions for a person's age, sex, and activity level.

A disease caused by the prolonged lack of a specific nutrient in the diet. Examples: scurvy (lack of Vitamin C), rickets (lack of Vitamin D), anaemia (lack of iron), night blindness (lack of Vitamin A).

A chemical test to detect the presence of starch in food. When iodine solution is added to a food sample containing starch, it turns blue-black. A negative result (no starch) leaves iodine orange-brown.

worked_examples.question: A student adds iodine solution to a boiled potato slice and to a piece of apple. The potato turns blue-black but the apple remains orange-brown. What do these results tell us?
step_by_step_answer: Step 1: Recall the iodine test — Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present. If there is no starch, iodine remains orange-brown.
Step 2: Interpret the potato result — Potato turned blue-black → starch is present in potato. This is expected since potato is a starchy vegetable.
Step 3: Interpret the apple result — Apple remained orange-brown → starch is NOT present in apple. Apple contains sugar (fructose) rather than starch as its carbohydrate.

Step 4: Draw conclusion — Starch is a type of carbohydrate found in foods like potato, rice, and wheat. Not all carbohydrates are starch — fruits like apple contain sugar, which is a different type of carbohydrate that does not react with iodine.
Conclusion: The iodine test confirms that potato contains starch (positive result) while apple does not (negative result), even though both contain carbohydrates.

worked_examples.question: Use the term 'deficiency disease' in a sentence connected to Vitamin D, and explain what the disease is.
step_by_step_answer: Step 1: Recall meaning — A deficiency disease is caused by long-term lack of a specific nutrient in the diet.
Step 2: Connect to Vitamin D — Vitamin D is needed for the body to absorb calcium and build strong bones. It is produced by the skin on exposure to sunlight and is found in milk and fish.
Step 3: Write sentence: 'Rickets is a deficiency disease caused by prolonged lack of Vitamin D in children — it causes the bones to become soft and bend, leading to bow legs or knock knees.'

worked_examples.question: Your friend says: 'I only eat rice and pickle every day — I feel fine.' Using your knowledge of nutrients, explain why this diet is dangerous in the long term.
step_by_step_answer: Step 1: State the lesson — A balanced diet must contain all nutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water, and roughage. Each nutrient has a function no other nutrient can perform.

Step 2: Analyse the diet — Rice provides carbohydrates. Pickle provides some salt (minerals) and spices. But this diet is missing: protein (for growth/repair), vitamins (for protection), dietary fat (for energy reserve and vitamin absorption), and roughage (for digestion).

Step 3: Apply — Long-term effects of this diet: protein deficiency → marasmus or kwashiorkor (muscle wasting); Vitamin C deficiency → scurvy (bleeding gums); Vitamin A deficiency → night blindness; iron deficiency → anaemia; lack of roughage → constipation.

Step 4: Conclusion — Feeling fine in the short term does not mean the diet is adequate. Deficiency diseases take weeks to months to appear. Your friend needs dal (protein), vegetables (vitamins, minerals, roughage), and some oil or ghee (fat) to have a complete, balanced diet.

questions.q: Which nutrient is the primary source of energy for the human body?
questions.a: Carbohydrates are the primary source of energy. They are broken down into glucose, which fuels all body cells.

questions.q: Name two food sources of protein.
questions.a: Dal (lentils), eggs, milk, meat, soya bean, cheese, and nuts are all protein sources. Any two are acceptable.

questions.q: Why do we need both carbohydrates AND fats if both provide energy?
questions.a: Carbohydrates provide quick, immediate energy that the body burns first. Fats provide a longer-lasting, concentrated reserve energy and also have other functions — insulating the body, protecting organs, and helping absorb fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Both are needed for different reasons.

questions.q: Why are vitamins needed in only very small amounts compared to carbohydrates?
questions.a: Vitamins act as regulators and catalysts — they help chemical reactions happen in the body but are not directly burned for energy or used as building material in large quantities. A small amount is enough to perform their specific protective and regulatory functions, unlike carbohydrates which are constantly burned for energy.

questions.q: Design a simple balanced meal using foods available in Karnataka that covers carbohydrates, protein, fat, and at least one vitamin.
questions.a: Sample answer: Ragi mudde (carbohydrate + calcium), sambar with toor dal (protein + Vitamin C from tomato), a teaspoon of ghee or coconut oil (fat), and a piece of papaya or guava for dessert (Vitamin C). This covers all major nutrient groups using locally available Karnataka foods.

key_takeaways: Food contains five major nutrients: carbohydrates (energy), proteins (body-building), fats (reserve energy), vitamins (protection), and minerals (structural functions).
Water and roughage are also essential components of a healthy diet, even though they are not nutrients in the strict sense.
Iodine test: blue-black colour = starch present. No colour change = starch absent.
Paper test: translucent (see-through) greasy patch = fat present.
Biuret test: violet/purple colour = protein present.
Deficiency diseases — each caused by a specific nutrient shortage: night blindness (Vit A), scurvy (Vit C), rickets (Vit D), anaemia (iron), goitre (iodine), kwashiorkor/marasmus (protein).
A balanced diet contains all nutrients in the right proportions — no single food can provide everything.
Roughage (dietary fibre) aids digestion and prevents constipation — found in whole grains, vegetables, and fruits.
Karnataka's traditional diet (ragi mudde + sambar + vegetables) is naturally balanced across major nutrients.
The Karnataka government addresses anaemia and Vitamin A deficiency through school meal programmes and supplementation.
